messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mele was raised in the United States in a tight-knit Pacific Islander family, and some of her earliest memories are of trying to read the adults in the house before she entered a room. When she was eight, she witnessed repeated violence by a man in the family home against someone she depended on and trusted to keep her safe. What stayed with her most was not a single blow but the charged stillness around it: the way everyone seemed to know and not say, the sound of her own heart hammering while she stood frozen outside a doorway, and the sickening confusion of hearing the perpetrator spoken to gently by name the next morning as if nothing had happened. As a child she did not have words for betrayal, but she understood that the people she relied on could watch suffering, conceal it, and expect her to carry on.

In the years afterward, the memories never settled into a clear past. At times Mele could describe what had happened in a flat, almost detached way, as if she were telling a story about someone else’s childhood, and that emotional blankness frightened her in its own right. At other times something in the environment would bring the whole scene back without warning, and when it did she was flooded not only with the image of the violence but with intense shame, as though remembering exposed something rotten in her. The memory itself seemed to tell her what it meant: that she had been betrayed by people she trusted, that there must have been something about her that made her the sort of child this could happen around, and that people were never as safe or as straightforward as they appeared.

Now 31 and working as a dancer, Mele lives in a world of mirrors, rehearsal directors, audiences, and constant observation, and that setting has made her reactions painfully concrete. If she hears a name that resembles the perpetrator’s, even in passing backstage or in casual conversation, she feels herself tense before she has fully registered why. When she becomes aware of being watched in rehearsal, especially when a room goes quiet and eyes are on her body, she can suddenly feel like the child outside that doorway again. If her heart starts racing during a difficult sequence, the sensation itself can set something off; her pounding chest becomes not just exertion but a signal that danger is already here. In those moments, the trigger does not stay a simple sound or bodily sensation. It instantly revives what she has come to believe about other people and about herself: that appearances cannot be trusted, that safety can be false, and that somehow she is implicated.

Those beliefs, in turn, keep her scanning for exactly those cues. Mele has come to move through rehearsals with a private vigilance, alert to who is looking at her, what names are being spoken, and any quick surge in her heartbeat. She is certain that people are not what they seem, so being watched rarely feels neutral; it feels like the prelude to being judged, exposed, or blindsided. Because she believes there is something in her that made the original violence possible, the physical rush of her own body does not read as ordinary nerves but as confirmation that she is vulnerable in some essential way. The more she lives inside those meanings, the more potent the cues become.

Over the past few years, this has narrowed her life. In the studio she sometimes loses whole moments of choreography when a passing remark or a sudden awareness of the room’s attention pulls the memory fully into the present. Afterward she may recount the childhood events with eerie numbness, then be hit minutes later by shame so strong she avoids eye contact with castmates. She does not describe broad fear of crowds or explicit panic; instead, it is these specific moments—hearing a related name, catching someone’s gaze, noticing her heart pounding under stage lights—that feel contaminated. Her husband has noticed that after certain rehearsals she becomes distant and guarded, quick to assume hidden motives in ordinary interactions.

Mele sought help after a recent rehearsal in which the director repeatedly called out a male understudy’s name, one close enough to the original name to make her body go cold. Standing in formation while the artistic staff watched, she felt her heart slam in her chest and was suddenly back in the house, overwhelmed by the certainty that trusted people can turn dangerous and that some part of her had invited what happened. She finished the run emotionally blank, then cried in the dressing room from shame she could not explain. What frightens her most is that these reactions are starting to govern the career she loves and the marriage she values. What she hopes for, cautiously, is not to erase the past, but to stop feeling that a name, a stare, or her own heartbeat can so easily tell her who she is and what the world is.
